Two of the seven land squarely on this passage: consuming *ribā*, which both Ibn Kathir and the Companions' reading of *bi'l-bāṭil* place under ayah 29's prohibition, and killing a life Allah has forbidden, which its third clause forbids.

In the Two Sahihs also, Ibn Masʿūd asked what the greatest sin was. He ﷺ said, "To make a rival for Allah while He alone created you." "Then?" — "To kill your offspring for fear that he might share your food with you." "Then?" — "To commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." The last is doubly grave, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, since protecting a neighbour's family is as binding as protecting one's own.

Two themes recur across the other narrations Ibn Kathir gathers. One is **false witness**: Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ named shirk, killing a soul and undutifulness to parents, then asked, "Should I tell you about the biggest of the major sins? The false statement — or the false testimony." Shuʿbah, one of the narrators, said that most likely, in his opinion, he said "false testimony"; the Two Sahihs recorded this hadith from Shuʿbah from Anas. The other is **the honour of parents** — ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr reported him ﷺ counting among the worst major sins that a man cause his own parents to be cursed, by cursing another's father and being answered in kind (the wording is Muslim's).

## Living it

The passage asks first where your wealth comes from, not only how you spend it, and Ibn Kathir's warning is that the danger lies in methods "that appear to be legal." So test a deal against Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's two conditions: is there real value on both sides, or only time, chance, or a promise standing in for a commodity — and is the other side's consent freely given, or squeezed out?

And note where ayah 31 leaves the reader. The catalogue of great sins is long and sobering, but it is set down as something to steer around — and Allah's answer to a life that steers around it is to erase what is small and open a noble door.

passages.title: Do not covet another's portion; every estate has its claimants
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These two ayat address the ache that follows any comparison: the feeling that someone else was given what should have been yours. Ayah 32 forbids coveting the portions Allah has distributed among people, redirects the heart from envy to asking Allah directly, and promises that no one's effort is lost. Ayah 33 then closes the circle on the practical case that provoked the question in the first place — inheritance — by affirming that Allah Himself has appointed the heirs to every estate.

What holds them together is the word *share*. Ayah 32 speaks of a share (*naṣīb*) earned by each man and woman; ayah 33 speaks of a share to be handed over to those to whom it is owed. In both, the portion is assigned — by Allah's wisdom in one case, by His law in the other — and the believer's task is not to redraw the lines but to be content, to work, and to ask.

## The moment of revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The rulings of inheritance had just been given, in which — under the stated conditions — a male receives a share equal to that of two females, and other aspects of male precedence had also been established. Sayyidah Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) said to the Prophet ﷺ words to the effect: *Our share in the inheritance is half. And there are such-and-such differences between us and men…*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful about how we read her: **her purpose was not to raise an objection.** She wished to be a man and so to deserve the merits reserved for men. Other women were wishing the same thing from a different angle: *had we been men, we would have taken part in jihād and the merit of jihād would have been ours.* And a woman asked the Prophet ﷺ whether, since a man receives a double share of inheritance and a woman's testimony counts as half a man's, women would also receive half the reward for all their acts of worship.

Ibn Kathir reports the same occasion from the hadith literature: **Imam Ahmad recorded** that Umm Salamah said, "O Messenger of Allah! Men go to battle, but we do not go to battle, and we earn one-half of the inheritance (that men get)" — and Allah sent down *wa lā tatamannaw mā faḍḍala-llāhu bihi baʿḍakum ʿalā baʿḍ*. **At-Tirmidhi also recorded this hadith.**

So the ayah answers two different questions at once, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes them precisely: the answer to Sayyidah Umm Salamah was given by *"and do not covet…"*, and the answer to the woman asking about reward was given by *"for men there is a share of what they earned…"* One half of the ayah says: stop wishing to be someone else. The other half says: nothing you actually do is discounted.

## "Do not covet" — what exactly is forbidden

The prohibition in ayah 32 is aimed at a specific kind of wishing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the line clearly: what is forbidden here is coveting **things, traits and merits given to others that are not acquirable by effort.**

The examples given are concrete: being born male, being born into a prophet's family or a ruler's family, being born beautiful. These, in the words of the commentary, are simply blessings of Allah's giving, outside anyone's reach. A woman cannot become a man. No one can choose the family he is born into. No one can genuinely change his physique into the face and frame he would have chosen — no matter, as the commentary puts it, how much he struggles with medicines, treatments and devices.

And here is the diagnosis. When a person finds himself lacking — in wealth, comfort, beauty, merit, knowledge — he feels a surge that pushes him to at least draw level with the other, if not to get ahead. When he discovers he cannot, the self begins to whisper a second thought: *how wonderful if that blessing were taken away from him too, so that he becomes equal to me, or lower.* **That is envy** — a shameful and destructive trait, and, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the cause of countless disputes, disturbances, killings and ravages in the world.

The ayah "closes the doors of disorders" at exactly this point. Allah, in His infinite wisdom, has distributed different merits to different people: this quality to one, that quality to another, less to some, more to others. The instruction is that each person rest pleased with what has been assigned to him and stay clear of the envious desire to possess another's excellences — because the end result of that game of desires is nothing but a biting sense of personal loss, and the sin of envy on top of it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then turns the principle over and looks at both sides of it, and this is worth sitting with:

- Whoever Allah has made a man should be grateful for it; whoever Allah has made a woman should be pleased with that, considering that had she been a man she might have failed the responsibilities placed on a man and ended up sinful.
- Whoever was created beautiful should be all the more grateful; whoever is lesser in looks should not grieve, since beauty carries no guarantee of good and may itself become a trial or a road to corruption.
- Whoever is a true lineal descendant of the Prophet ﷺ should thank Allah for that connection; whoever is not should neither worry nor pine for it, because it cannot be acquired by effort — and insisting on coveting it yields only sin, a broken heart and an aching soul.

The alternative is put in one line: rather than pine for a lineage you do not have, **think about your own doings.** Let them be good and righteous. A person who builds himself with such spiritual strength, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, can be ahead of those with higher or better lineage.

## The competition that is *encouraged*

This is the essential qualification, and the commentary insists on it: **striving to excel others in good deeds is a different matter entirely.** There are ayat of the Qur'an and sayings of the Prophet ﷺ that exhort people to excel one another in good deeds. That field is open. Looking at the trail of merits and excellence others have left is permitted there — indeed, people have been persuaded to make every possible effort to acquire them.

The difference is control. Deeds within a person's control — those acquired by learning, training and working — are within reach. If someone is impressed by another's intellectual merits, practical life and excellent morals, he may by all means strive to acquire those qualities; that is very desirable and praiseworthy, and the ayah does not contradict it.

In fact the later part of ayah 32 supports it: *for men there is a share of what they earned, and for women there is a share of what they earned.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the hint: effort and struggle in acquiring merits and perfections **do not go to waste**; every man and woman will certainly receive a return, a share of his or her own effort.

Ibn Kathir records two readings of this same phrase. According to Ibn Jarīr, it indicates that each person earns the wages of his works — reward if his deeds are good, punishment if they are evil. It was also reported, as Al-Walibi related from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the ayah is speaking of inheritance, indicating that each person receives his due share of it.

So the passage sorts two failures at once, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays them out:

**The first failure** is the person who becomes so devoted to acquiring what cannot be acquired that he ruins an otherwise peaceful life in this world — and if that curdles into envy, wishing the blessing removed from the one who has it, then his chances of salvation in the life to come are destroyed too by that grave sin.

**The second failure** is the opposite: the person who lacks courage, avoids action, has no sense of honour or shame, and does not even try for the merits that *can* be acquired — and who, when approached with good counsel, immediately blames destiny and fate, which is no more than a way of camouflaging his own timidity and inertia.

The ayah resolves both with a wise and just rule. What lies outside a person's control — being high-born, being handsome — should be resigned to fate; one must be content with the divinely determined state he is in and grateful to Allah. Coveting beyond that is, in the commentary's phrase, absurd, ineffectual and meddlesome, leaving behind nothing but a handful of sorrows. What can be acquired by effort is worth wishing for **only if the wish is supported by the necessary struggle to achieve it** — and the ayah carries the promise that the effort so made will not be wasted.

## Why this comes right after the warning against devouring wealth and killing

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Tafsir al-Bahr al-Mishit on the placement. Ayah 29 had prohibited the unjust use of someone's property and the unjust taking of someone's life. This ayah, al-Bahr al-Mishit points out, **aims to seal the very source of those crimes** — which is why the instruction is to stop people from coveting those who are ahead of them in wealth, comfort or influence.

Think it through, as the commentary does. Theft, robbery, other illegitimate ways of usurping property, killing and destruction — these all sprout from one particular emotional attitude. A man finds another ahead of him in wealth or material acquisition. First comes the pinch in the heart, the wish to come at par with him or even to surpass him. Then the intensity of that desire pushes him all the way to committing the crime. The Qur'an blocks the source of these crimes by blocking the desire that feeds them.

## "And ask Allah of His bounty"

Having closed one door, ayah 32 opens a better one: *was'alū-llāha min faḍlih.*

Ibn Kathir renders the logic of the ayah as a direct address from Allah: do not wish for what other people were endowed with over you, for that is a decision that will come to pass and wishing does not change its decree — **but ask Me of My favour and I will grant it to you, for I am Most Generous and Most Giving.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the wording. When you see someone excel in one or another of the graces of life, the ideal conduct is not to wish to come at par with him in that particular excellence, but to pray to Allah asking for His graces and blessings. The reason given is that Allah's grace appears in a different form for every person. For some, wealth is the blessing, because had they become paupers they might have fallen victim to sin and disbelief. For others the blessing lies precisely in the straitened circumstances they are in, because had they turned rich they might have succumbed to thousands of sins. For some, grace appears as power and influence; for others — the unremembered and the unattended — the grace of Allah is manifest in that very state, since power and influence might have caused them to fall into many a sin.

So the instruction is: when you ask Allah, do not ask for some fixed quality of life. Ask for **His** grace, so that He, in His infinite wisdom, opens the doors of His blessings upon you.

There is something quietly transformative in that redirection. The restlessness that would otherwise be spent measuring yourself against a neighbour is spent instead on asking the One who distributes.

## "Indeed Allah is ever All-Knowing of everything"

The ayah closes on a name of Allah, and both commentaries treat this as the foundation the whole prohibition rests on.

Ibn Kathir explains: Allah knows who deserves this life, and so gives him riches; and whoever deserves poverty, He makes him poor. He also knows who deserves the Hereafter, and directs him to the deeds that will help him succeed in it; and whoever deserves failure, He prevents him from achieving righteousness and what leads to it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion from the other end: the hint in this closing phrase is that the arrangement of things made by Allah is the very quintessence of wisdom and justice. Whoever has been created and sustained in whatever condition — that arrangement is perfectly matched with the ideal demand of wisdom and justice. **But man is not fully aware of the consequences of what he does.** This is something only Allah knows best, and so He alone knows how suitable it is to keep anyone in a given condition.

## Ayah 33: every estate already has its claimants

*And to everyone We have appointed mawālī of what parents and relatives leave behind.*

**Mawālī.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Abu Salih, Qatādah, Zayd bin Aslam, As-Suddī, Ad-Daḥḥāk, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān and others all explained *mawālī* here to mean **heirs**. Ibn ʿAbbās was also reported to have said that it refers to relatives, and Ibn Jarīr commented that the Arabs call the cousin a *mawlā*.

Ibn Jarīr reads the phrase *of what parents and relatives leave* as meaning: from what a person himself inherited from his parents and family members. So the meaning of the ayah becomes, in his words: *to all of you, O people, We appointed relatives — such as children — who will later inherit what you inherited from your own parents and relatives.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this restatement of inheritance appears at just this point. The background was that some women, on learning that men were given a share equal to that of two women, wished they were men so that they too would receive a doubled share. So the law of inheritance is reiterated here and it is said, tersely, that **all the shares determined in it are based on perfect wisdom and justice.** Since human reason cannot encompass the totality of factors that contribute to the order or disorder of the created universe, it cannot arrive precisely at the elements of wisdom taken into consideration in determining the laws of Allah. Therefore: whoever has been allotted whatever share should be pleased with it and grateful for it.

## The pledge of brotherhood, and what became of it

The end of ayah 33 — *and those with whom your right hands have made a pledge, give them their due portion* — preserves a moment from the earliest years of Islam.

**Al-Bukhari recorded** that Ibn ʿAbbās said: when the emigrants came to Al-Madinah, the emigrant would inherit from the Anṣārī while the Anṣārī's own relatives would not inherit from him, because of the bond of brotherhood the Prophet ﷺ had established between them. When *"and to everyone We have appointed mawālī"* was revealed, it cancelled the pledge of brotherhood with respect to inheritance.

Ibn ʿAbbās then adds the crucial nuance: the phrase *"give them their due portion"* **remained valid for cases of cooperation and mutual advice**, while the matter of inheritance was excluded from it — and it became permissible to assign something in one's will to the person who had the right of inheriting before.

Ibn Kathir gives the same sequence: this practice was followed at the beginning of Islam, but was later abrogated when Muslims were commanded to fulfil the pledges they had already given and to refrain from making any new ones after that. Allah, he notes, witnessed all of them when they gave those pledges and promises — which is why the ayah ends *"Truly Allah is ever a Witness over all things."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concurs that this share on the basis of a pledge belonged to the initial period of Islam, and states that it was later abrogated by the verse *"as for the womb-relatives, some of them are closer to some…"* (33:6). The settled position: **if other heirs exist, a pledge or mutual contract between two parties does not affect the inheritance in any manner whatsoever.**

## Living it

**Sort your longings into two piles.** One pile is what cannot be acquired by effort — your birth, your lineage, your form. Resign that to Allah's decree, be content with it and grateful for it; coveting beyond that leaves behind nothing but a handful of sorrows, and wishing the blessing away from the one who has it is envy, a grave sin. The other pile is what learning, training and work can win — knowledge, character, good morals, righteous deeds. Want those, and then back the wish with the struggle, because the ayah promises that the effort will not be wasted.

**Watch for the second thought.** The first pang of noticing that someone has more is the surge the commentary describes. The sin begins where the heart moves from *I wish I had that* to *I wish he did not.* Catch it there.

**Turn the glance upward.** When you see someone excelling in some grace of life, do not wish to come level with him in that particular thing — pray to Allah for His grace, and let His wisdom open whichever doors of blessing are truly good for you.

**And do not use "destiny" as an alibi.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names this failure plainly: people who will not even attempt what is achievable and then blame destiny and fate, camouflaging their own timidity and inertia. This passage forbids the wrong ambition; it does not excuse having none.

passages.title: Order and responsibility in the household
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Ayah 34 lays down the working constitution of a Muslim household: who carries responsibility for it, on what grounds, what a righteous wife's part in it looks like, and what a husband may and may not do when the marriage begins to break down. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the verses just before this one forbade men to withhold or waste women's rights; ayah 34 now turns to the other side of the ledger and states the rights of men. The unit holds together because it moves in one continuous line: a principle (men are *qawwāmūn*), its two stated reasons, the portrait of the wife who lives by it, and a graded procedure for the wife who does not — closing with a warning aimed squarely at the husband himself.

## The background of the revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān first records a historical note, on the authority of Ibn Saʿd and al-Bayhaqī, from the daughter of Sayyidnā Abū Bakr (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu): the beating of women was absolutely prohibited in the early days, but this resulted in some women becoming much too oppressive, following which the permission was reinstated.

It then records an event it calls the background of this revelation. Sayyidnā Zayd ibn Zuhayr (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) had married his daughter, Sayyidah Ḥabībah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhā), to Sayyidnā Saʿd ibn Rabīʿ (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu). During a dispute over something, the husband slapped her. Ḥabībah complained to her father; he took her to the Prophet ﷺ, who declared that Ḥabībah had the right to strike Saʿd as hard as he had struck her. Hearing this decision of their master, they started back home to take that retaliation — and thereupon this verse was revealed. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the verse permitted the beating of women only as the very last option, and allowed no retaliation or revenge against men. Soon after its revelation the Prophet ﷺ called both of them back, asked them to abide by the injunction from Allah, and abrogated his first directive permitting the seeking of revenge.

## "Qawwāmūn" — the key word

*Al-rijālu qawwāmūna ʿalā al-nisāʾ*: "Men are the caretakers of women."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up. In Arabic, *qawwām* (also *qayyām*, *qayyim*) denotes a person who holds the responsibility, who has the duty and charge to manage a job, run a system, or take care of what needs doing — controlling all the related factors involved. It has been rendered in several ways: most commonly as *ḥākim*, one who rules, governs or decides; also as guardian, custodian, overseer, protector. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful about which sense is meant: the *qawwām* of the Qurʼān is a carer and a functional head, **not** a ruler or dictator in the political sense.

Ibn Kathir glosses it in the same register: the man is responsible for the woman; he is her maintainer, caretaker and leader, who disciplines her if she deviates.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then argues the point from ordinary experience. Any group living together, large or small, and any organised system, rationally and customarily needs a head or chief or authority — someone who can arbitrate in the event of a difference and take decisions so that affairs run smoothly. This is universally accepted and practised for countries, governments and states, and the same need was felt in older tribal societies, where the chief of a tribe was taken as the authority for that tribe. Why would a family organisation — a micro-sample of the larger organisations — not need someone to head, maintain and run the system? Allah, in His infinite wisdom, elected men for this responsibility because their natural capabilities are more pronounced than those of women and children.

And the authority is fenced in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that, as other verses of the Qurʼān explain, this mantle is not that of a dictator and a tyrant. In exercising it the man is bound by the supreme law of Islam, the Sharīʿah; he must act on the principle of consultation and follow good counsel; he simply cannot act on the spur of his whim. The command given to him is *wa ʿāshirūhunna bil-maʿrūf* — treat women well, in the recognised, decent way. And 2:233 speaks of decisions made *ʿan tarāḍin minhumā wa tashāwur* — by mutual consent and consultation, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads as an instruction to men to act in consultation with their wives in family affairs.

## The two reasons given

Allah does not simply announce the arrangement; He gives two grounds for it, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that one relates to the wisdom of creation, beyond the control of any human being, while the other comes through a person's own effort and endeavour.

**First:** *bimā faḍḍala Allāhu baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍ* — "as Allah has made some of them excel others." Ibn Kathir explains this as men excelling over women and being better suited for certain tasks; this, he says, is why prophethood was exclusive to men, as were other important positions of leadership. He cites the ḥadīth of the Prophet ﷺ, **recorded by al-Bukhārī**: *"People who appoint a woman to be their leader will never achieve success."* Ibn Kathir applies this to appointing women as judges or to other positions of leadership.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the same clause as a matter of divine allotment rather than merit. It compares it to the way Allah declared a particular House of Worship in the sacred environs of Makkah to be His House and the Qiblah, and gave a special honour to Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem. Men have done nothing to get this grace, and there is nothing wrong with women that they do not have it; it rests simply on the wisdom of creation, an exclusive privilege of the Creator.

**Second:** *wa bimā anfaqū min amwālihim* — "and because they spend of their wealth." Ibn Kathir specifies: the dowry, the expenditures and the various expenses that Allah ordained in His Book and in the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ for men to spend on women. For these reasons, he says, it is suitable that the husband is appointed her maintainer — as Allah said, *"But men have a degree over them"* (2:228).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes a remark of Ibn Ḥibbān in *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* that is worth pausing over: these two reasons also prove that **the right to authority is not established simply by force**; rather, it is deserved on the basis of one's competence and capability.

## Why "some of them over others" and not "men over women"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a deliberate turn of phrase. The Qurʼān did not say *faḍḍalahum ʿalayhinna* — "because He made *men* excel *women*." It chose instead *baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍ* — "made some of them excel the others." The wisdom, it says, is not difficult to see: the expression subtly indicates that men and women are part of each other. So whatever precedence men have, even if proved in one field or another, goes no further than the precedence of a man's head over his hand, or of his heart over his stomach. Just as the head's precedence does not diminish the role and importance of the hand, so this precedence causes no lowering of the status of women — if man is the head, woman is the body.

Some commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, identify a further hint: this precedence is in terms of *genus*. As far as individuals are concerned, it is quite possible for a woman to excel a man in her qualities and practical accomplishments — so much so that a woman may be superior to some individual men even in the qualities of a caretaker.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also connects this to inheritance. The declaration that all financial responsibility rests with men removes the doubt that may creep up because a man's share is twice a woman's: before marriage a woman's expenses rest with her father, after marriage they pass to her husband, so the twofold share "zooms back to women after all." Its conclusion is explicit: there is no value judgment being made here — this is no more than a functional distribution of duties, and no lowering of women's status.

## The profile of the righteous wife

*Fa-l-ṣāliḥātu qānitātun ḥāfiẓātun lil-ghaybi bimā ḥafiẓa Allāh.*

**Qānitāt.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and others that this means obedient to their husbands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the phrase as a whole: righteous women accept this rule of the precedence of men and obey them, and when the husbands are not with them they stand guard over their own selves and over what the husband has earned for the family.

**Ḥāfiẓātun lil-ghayb.** As-Suddī and others, as Ibn Kathir relays, said this means she protects her honour and her husband's property when he is absent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a fine observation: this duty is not restricted to when the husband is away — it applies equally during his presence. The Qurʼān mentions his absence in express terms because that is when a woman is more susceptible to showing negligence. What has to be avoided is showing a lot of concern and alertness while the husband is in the house and neglecting these rules of conduct when he is out of sight.

**Bimā ḥafiẓa Allāh.** Ibn Kathir reports the meaning as: the protected one is the one whom Allah protects. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as a declaration of divine help: these responsibilities are not easy to take care of, and Allah declares immediately after naming them that He helps women when they so protect. It is with His support — the *tawfīq* of Allah, His enabling grace — that they succeed in grappling with these heavy responsibilities, since the temptations of the self and of Satan stand surrounding every man and woman all the time.

### From the Sunnah on this

- Ibn Jarīr recorded that Abū Hurayrah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The best of women is she who, when you look at her, she pleases you; when you command her, she obeys you; and when you are absent, she protects her honour and your property."* The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then recited this ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays the same ḥadīth as, most probably, an explanation of this very verse.
- **Imām Aḥmad** recorded that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"If the woman prayed her five daily prayers, fasted her month, protected her chastity and obeyed her husband, she will be told: enter Paradise from any of its doors you wish."*
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* that the Prophet ﷺ said that for a woman who is dutiful to her husband, there are birds in the air, fish in the sea, angels in the skies and beasts in the forests who pray for her forgiveness by her Lord.

## Nushūz, and the three graded steps

*Wa-llātī takhāfūna nushūzahunna.* Ibn Kathir defines *nushūz* concretely: ill conduct towards her husband — acting as though she is above him, disobeying him, ignoring him, showing dislike of him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as outright disobedience, or failure to cooperate with the husband in running family affairs in the recognised manner.

When these signs appear, Ibn Kathir says, the husband should advise her and remind her of Allah. He grounds the seriousness of the matter in the weight of the husband's rights: Allah ordered the wife to obey her husband and prohibited her from disobeying him because of the enormity of his rights and all that he does for her. In that connection Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ as saying that if he were to command anyone to prostrate to anyone, he would have commanded the wife to prostrate to her husband, because of the enormity of his right upon her. (Ibn Kathir names no collection for this wording.) He then cites al-Bukhārī, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said that if a man asks his wife to come to his bed and she declines, the angels keep cursing her until the morning; and Muslim recorded it with the wording that if a wife goes to sleep while shunning her husband's bed, the angels keep cursing her until the morning.

Both commentaries insist the three responses are **sequential** — to be followed in the order in which they are mentioned — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole thing as a compact system designed to settle the trouble within the four walls of the house, without any third party having to intercede.

**1. *Faʿiẓūhunna* — admonish.** Ibn Kathir: the husband should advise her and remind her of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: talk it over with her nicely and softly, in a way that helps change her mind and attitude. If that works, the issue is resolved right there — the woman is rescued from a permanent sin, the man from an aching heart, and the two of them from ever-stinging anguish.

**2. *Wahjurūhunna fī al-maḍājiʿ* — withdraw in the beds.** Ibn Kathir reports through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa that Ibn ʿAbbās said the abandonment means not having intercourse with her, lying on her bed with his back to her; several others said similarly. As-Suddī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah, and Ibn ʿAbbās in another narration added: not speaking with her. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qurʼān says *in the beds* — and it is from here that the Muslim jurists deduced that this staying apart is limited to the beds and not to the house itself. The woman should not be left alone in the house, something bound to hurt her feelings much more and to make further straining of relations far more likely. This is backed by the report Ibn Kathir attributes to **the Sunan and Musnad compilers**, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥaydah al-Qushayrī, who asked, "O Allah's Messenger! What is the right that the wife of one of us has on him?" The Prophet ﷺ said: *"To feed her when you eat, clothe her when you buy clothes for yourself, refrain from striking her face or cursing her, and to not abandon her, except in the house."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same report from *Mishkāt*.

**3. *Waḍribūhunna*.** Ibn Kathir: if advice and ignoring her in the bed do not produce the desired results, one is allowed to discipline the wife — **without severe beating**. He cites Muslim, from Jābir, from the Farewell Ḥajj, where the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Fear Allah regarding women, for they are your assistants. You have the right on them that they do not allow any person whom you dislike to step on your mat. However, if they do that, you are allowed to discipline them lightly. They have a right on you that you provide them with their provision and clothes, in a reasonable manner."* Ibn Kathir then records that Ibn ʿAbbās and several others said the ayah refers to a beating that is not violent, and that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said it means a beating that is not severe.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is stronger still. It calls this "token" beating, permitted only as a last resort and as a forced option in a particular mode — in a manner that does not affect the body, and that goes nowhere near the undesirable limits of hurt or injury to skin or bones. **Slapping or hitting on the face is absolutely forbidden.** It notes that right alongside this option it appears in ḥadīth that *good men among you will never beat women*; that the use of this measure was not liked by the Prophet ﷺ, who said on the contrary that gentlemen would not do that; and that such an action is nowhere reported from the blessed prophets of Allah. The first two steps, it says, are more or less an exercise in nobility against arrogant lack of compromise — something the prophets and their righteous followers both spoke in favour of and practised.

## "Do not seek a way against them"

*Fa-in aṭaʿnakum falā tabghū ʿalayhinna sabīlā.* Ibn Kathir: when the wife obeys her husband in all that Allah has allowed, then no means of annoyance from the husband are allowed against her at all — in that case he does not have the right to beat her or to shun her bed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: should the women mend themselves after that triple-stepped approach, men should forgive and forgo the past and avoid hair-splitting or levelling fresh accusations over flimsy issues.

Then the seal: *Inna Allāha kāna ʿAliyyan Kabīrā* — "Indeed Allah is Ever Most High, Most Great." Ibn Kathir reads this as a reminder to men: if they transgress against their wives without justification, then Allah, the Ever Most High, the Most Great, is their wives' Protector, and He will exert revenge on those who transgress against them and deal with them unjustly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in the same key — the measure of precedence over women given to you by Allah is not absolute, for the precedence of Allah hangs heavy over you; if you exceed the limits set for you, it is you who is going to take the punishment.

## Living it

Read as the two commentaries read it, this passage asks something of both spouses and something more of the one holding authority. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary is worth carrying: the rights of women are as incumbent upon men as the rights of men are upon women, with the single exception that men have a certain precedence in functional authority — and even that is hemmed in by other balancing factors: by the Sharīʿah, by consultation, by *ʿāshirūhunna bil-maʿrūf*, and by the certainty of answering to Allah. Great care, it says, has been taken to ensure that the rights of women are duly fulfilled, precisely because they cannot wrest their rights from men by using physical power.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points forward. The arrangement in ayah 34 is meant to help tempers cool off within the privacy of the house, kept between the married couple. But there are times when the family feud becomes long-drawn — whether because a wife is temperamentally obstinate, or because a husband has been unjustly oppressive — and such a tussle will not remain within the four walls of the house. Supporters of one party go about maligning the other with all sorts of accusations, and what started as the disagreement of two individuals turns into a confrontation between two families. That is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns next: to the role of the family arbitrator in disputes.

passages.title: Arbiters when a marriage fractures
passages.tafsir:
## What this ayah is about

Ayah 35 addresses the moment a marriage has moved past private friction into open rupture — and instead of sending the couple to court, it sends two people from the two families to sit with them. In Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"If you fear a breach between the two, appoint (two) arbitrators, one from his family and the other from her's; if they both wish for peace, Allah will cause their reconciliation. Indeed Allah is Ever All-Knower, Well-Acquainted with all things."*

The ayah holds together as one movement: a fear diagnosed, a remedy prescribed, a promise of unseen help attached to sincerity, and a closing warning that the arbitrators themselves stand under the gaze of the All-Knowing.

## Where it sits in the flow

Ibn Kathir points out the sequence deliberately. Allah "first mentioned the case of rebellion on the part of the wife" — the situation dealt with just before — and "then mentioned the case of estrangement and alienation between the two spouses." So the earlier ayah handles a one-sided problem inside the home; ayah 35 handles the case where the breach is *mutual*, where blame cannot be cleanly assigned to one side, and where the trouble has grown too large for the couple alone to contain.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the two ayat together as a graded system. The Qur'an, it says, is here trying "to block the road to this terrible discord" — because a dispute of this kind "could not remain restricted to the couple's home." The aim is that it "at least be settled within their families and not go to a court of law to become public knowledge."

## "If you fear" — and who is being addressed

The ayah does not wait for the marriage to collapse. It moves at the stage of *fear* — before the split has fully arrived. And the address is plural: *"If you fear…"* — not spoken to the husband, not to the wife, but to a wider circle.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies that circle: the Qur'an "addresses government authorities of the time, the guardians of the parties concerned and their supporters, and the general body of Muslims." The responsibility to intervene is therefore not the couple's own. It rests on those around them who have standing: "concerned officials of the government or the guardians of the parties or a body of Muslims which has the necessary integrity, influence and authority should take charge and appoint two arbitrators."

That is worth sitting with. On this reading, a community that watches a marriage disintegrate and treats it as none of its business has stepped outside what the ayah asks of it. The ayah assumes that somebody with standing steps forward.

## Why the word *ḥakam*

The Arabic word the Qur'an chooses for the two appointees is **ḥakam** — used at both points in the ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this word choice as the ayah's own job description: "the Holy Qur'an has used the word, 'ḥakam' for these appointees whereby it pin-points the necessary qualifications of these two persons, that is, they should have the capability to decide the dispute between the two parties; and this capability, as obvious, will be found in a person who is both knowledgeable and trustworthy."

So a *ḥakam* is not merely a sympathetic ear. He is someone with the capability to *decide* the matter. Two qualities are demanded together: knowledge and trustworthiness. Ibn ʿAbbas, in the report narrated from him by Ali bin Abi Talhah, describes each appointee simply as "a righteous man" from each side.

**One from his family, one from hers.** The symmetry is the point. Each spouse sees somebody in the room who knows them and who cannot be dismissed as a stranger. And because both arbitrators are family, the dispute stays, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "settled within their families" rather than becoming public knowledge.

## The procedure the jurists drew from it

Ibn Kathir reports the practical shape the Fuqahāʼ — whom he glosses as "scholars of Fiqh" — gave this: "when estrangement occurs between the husband and wife, the judge refers them to a trusted person who examines their case in order to stop any wrongs committed between them. If the matter continues or worsens, the judge sends a trustworthy person from the woman's family and a trustworthy person from the man's family to meet with them and examine their case to determine whether it is best for them to part or to remain together."

Note that even the arbitrators are the *second* step. A single trusted person is tried first; only if the trouble continues or worsens are the two arbitrators sent.

## "If they both wish for peace, Allah will cause their reconciliation"

This is the heart of the ayah, and two things are drawn from it.

**First, Allah's own preference is stated.** Ibn Kathir writes plainly: "Allah gives preference to staying together, and this is why Allah said, *if they both wish for peace, Allah will cause their reconciliation*." The arbitration is not a neutral machine for processing a divorce. It leans, by design, toward repair.

**Second, success is tied to sincerity, and the help is unseen.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the two who "wish for peace" here to be the two arbitrators, and draws out: "If both arbitrators have good intentions and genuinely wish to bring about peace between the dissenting couple, there will be unseen help from Allah Almighty and they shall succeed in their mission, and it will be through their efforts that Allah Almighty will create love and harmony in the hearts of the couple."

Then it turns the statement around into something searching: "in cases where mutual rapport is not restored, it may be because one of the arbitrators lacks perfect sincerity while pursuing the goal of peace-making."

That is a hard mirror to hold up. When family mediation fails, the reflex is to blame the couple. Read this way, the ayah asks the mediator to examine his own heart first: did he go in genuinely wanting these two reconciled, or to win for his side of the family? The love and harmony in the hearts of the couple are, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, what "Allah Almighty will create." The arbitrator's contribution is his sincerity.

## What authority do the arbitrators actually have?

Here the scholars genuinely differed, and the sources set the disagreement out clearly.

**The Qur'an leaves it open.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid: once the two are sent, "as for what they are going to do when they meet them and as to what rights they have in this matter — this the Holy Qur'an does not determine."

**The position of Hasan al-Basri and Imam Abu Hanifah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that "the purpose of appointing these two arbitrators… is to bring about peace and amity between the husband and the wife and does not include anything beyond that." They have no inherent power to end the marriage. But if the couple appoints them "as their representatives and their attorneys in all respects," admitting in advance that any joint decision binds them, then "the two arbitrators shall have absolute authority to decide their case. If both agree on divorce as the solution, they can effect a divorce. If they both decide that the woman should be released under *khulʿ*" — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes as "a form of dissolution of marriage" — "the *khulʿ* shall come into effect, and their decision shall be binding on the parties." This is cited from Ruh al-Maʿani.

**The other view.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that from the incident with Sayyidna ʿAli (below), "some mujtahid Imams deduced the principle that these arbitrators have an inherent authority to divorce."

**Points of agreement.** Ibn Kathir cites Shaykh Abu ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-Barr: "The scholars agree that when the two arbitrators disagree, then the opinion that dissolves the marriage will not be adopted." That is a safeguard — a split verdict can never break a marriage. He adds that the scholars also agree the arbitrators' decision is binding "even if the two spouses did not appoint them as agents" where the decision is that the couple should stay together; whether it binds when they decide on separation was disputed, and "the majority holds the view that the decision is still binding."

**Ibn ʿAbbas's detailed report.** Ali bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the two righteous men are appointed "so that they find out who among the spouses is in the wrong. If the man is in the wrong, they prevent him from his wife, and he pays some restitution. If the wife is in the wrong, she remains with her husband, and he does not pay any restitution." Ibn ʿAbbas continues that whether they rule for the marriage to remain intact or to be dissolved, "their decision is upheld," and adds a case about inheritance where one spouse accepts the ruling to stay together and the other refuses. Ibn Kathir notes this was collected by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir.

## The case brought before Sayyidna ʿAli

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates an incident narrated by ʿUbaidah al-Salmani, which it says appears in the Sunan of al-Baihaqi.

A man and a woman came to Sayyidna ʿAli (may Allah honour his face), each with a group of people accompanying them. He asked them to appoint an arbitrator from the man's family and another from the woman's. When the arbitrators were appointed, he addressed them both: *"Do you know your responsibility? Do you know what you have to do? Hear me. If both of you agree to keep the husband and wife together and make peace between them, then do it. And if you come to the conclusion that matters cannot be set right between them or that they will not stay right later on, and both of you concur with the option that a separation between them is the expedient course, then do it."*

The woman answered at once: *"I accept this. Let these two arbitrators act in accordance with Divine law and I shall accept any decision they give whether it meets my wishes or goes against."*

The husband would not match her. He said: *"Separation and divorce are things I am not going to accept under any condition. However, I authorize the arbitrators to ask me to pay whatever financial penalty they impose and let my wife return to me in peace."* He was willing to be fined; he was not willing to be judged.

Sayyidna ʿAli refused the half-measure: *"No. You too should authorize the arbitrators in the same manner as was done by the woman."*

**Why this incident matters to the legal question.** Both camps read it. Those who hold the arbitrators have inherent power to divorce point to ʿAli instructing them that they may separate the couple. Imam Abu Hanifah and Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on them both) reason the opposite way: "had it been an inherent power of the arbitrators to divorce there was no need for Sayyidna ʿAli to obtain the authorization from the parties concerned. Here, the very effort to seek the agreement of the parties is a proof of the fact that these arbitrators do not have such an inherent power. Nevertheless, they do become authorized if the husband and wife delegate the necessary authority to them."

## Beyond the marriage: arbitration as a general principle

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that "Muslim jurists say that the appointment of two arbitrators to make peace between two parties in dispute is not limited to the disputes between a husband and a wife. It can be profitably used in other areas of discord" — and especially where the parties are related, "because a court decision is a short-term solution of the basic problem," leaving behind "the germs of hatred and hostility in the hearts of those affected."

It cites an order Sayyidna ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) promulgated for his judges: *"Send disputes between relatives back to them so that they make peace with the help of each other, as a court decision breeds heart burnings and hostility"* (cited from Muʿin al-Hukkam, p. 214). And it notes that although the directive concerns relatives, the *reason* given — that court decisions tend to create hatred and hostility in hearts — covers non-relatives as well. Hence the jurists' view that officials and judges "before hearing the cases formally, should make an effort to find a way out whereby the disputing parties get together and agree on mutual conciliation."

## The system in three stages

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises what these ayat build:

1. **Resolve family disputes within the house**, using one method after the other.
2. **When that is not possible**, government officials or kinsfolk make peace through two arbitrators, "so that, the dispute does not go out of the larger family circle, even if it goes out of the house itself."
3. **When that too is not possible** and the matter goes to the court, it is the duty of the judicial authority to investigate the case background of both parties and come up with a decision which is just.

Each stage tries to keep the wound from spreading. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees the stakes as larger than one household: if put into practice, this "could help eliminate a lot of disputes, hatreds and hostilities from the world," letting men and women "live in peace among their families, secure against all those local dissensions which turn into all sorts of tribal, racial, national, even, international feuds."

## The closing names — and who they are aimed at

The ayah ends: *"Indeed Allah is Ever All-Knower, Well-Acquainted with all things"* — rendered by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "Surely, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes precisely who is meant to feel the weight of these names here: "warning has been given to the two arbitrators as well to the effect that they should keep in mind that no injustice or crookedness from them will go unnoticed for they shall be appearing before the Being who knows all and is aware of everything."

It is an exact ending. The arbitrator may hold real weight over two people's lives at their most vulnerable, and he arrives carrying ties to one side of the family. Nobody in the room may ever detect a quiet bias in how he framed a question or which grievance he let slide. But, as the passage says, no crookedness from him will go unnoticed.

## Living it

- **Do not wait for the collapse.** The ayah triggers on *fear* of a breach, not on its arrival. Early is the point.
- **If you are close to a fracturing marriage, you are addressed.** The ayah speaks to guardians, to officials, and to "the general body of Muslims" — not to the couple alone.
- **Choose a *ḥakam*, not a partisan.** Knowledge and trustworthiness are the stated qualifications. Someone who arrives to win for "our side" has already fallen short of them.
- **Go in wanting reconciliation, and know that repair is not yours to manufacture.** Bring sincerity; it is Allah who creates the love and harmony in their hearts.
- **Take the ruling even when it goes against you.** The woman before Sayyidna ʿAli accepted a decision "whether it meets my wishes or goes against" — and ʿAli required the same unconditional authorization from her husband, who had offered only a conditional one.
- **Reach for conciliation before litigation generally**, especially among relatives — because, as Sayyidna ʿUmar's directive warns, a court decision "breeds heart burnings and hostility."

passages.title: Worship Allah alone and shun arrogant miserliness
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are one argument: ayah 36 commands the worship of Allah alone and lists eight kinds of people who have a claim on you; ayat 37–39 name the two faults that make a person fail that list, then ask what it would have cost him not to. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the thread: human rights have been this sūrah's focus from its opening — orphans, women, inheritance — and now come the rights of parents, relatives, neighbours and people at large, rights perfectly fulfilled only by someone whose orientation towards Allah, His Messenger and the answerability of the Last Day is correct and strong, and who avoids miserliness, arrogance and affectation, the impediments to all positive effort.

## Why worship comes first

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks why a roster of human rights opens with "Worship Allah and associate none with Him." What forces a person to honour other people's rights, *watched or unwatched*, is the fear of Allah and the sense of responsibility before Him; one neglectful there will always find an excuse — to satisfy his immediate circle, keep his prestige in society, or escape the law of the government. That taqwā (consciousness of Allah) is achieved through nothing but tawḥīd: firm belief in the Oneness of Allah, to the total exclusion of everything else from that unicity.

Ibn Kathir gives a complementary reason: Allah alone is the Creator and Sustainer who sends His favours and bounties on His creation in all situations, so He alone deserves to be singled out. He cites the Prophet's ﷺ exchange with Muʿādh: "Do you know what Allah's right on His servants is?" Muʿādh replied, "Allah and His Messenger know better." He said, "That they should worship Him and should not worship any others with Him." Then: "Do you know what the right of the servants on Allah is if they do this? He should not punish them." (Ibn Kathir names no collection.)

## Parents: the word is *iḥsān*

Ibn Kathir cites "give thanks to Me and to your parents" (31:14) and "your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be dutiful to your parents" (17:23); Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites 31:14 and the covenant of the Children of Isrāʾīl, "You shall not worship anyone but Allah; and to parents you shall be good" (2:83). Ibn Kathir explains the placement: Allah made parents the reason for the servants to come into existence after they did not exist. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in worldly terms the favours closest after Allah's own are a parent's: in the chain of causation they are the fountainhead of one's being, and from birth to youth they took care of one's existence, sustenance and growth to the best of their ability and means.

The word chosen is not "fulfil their rights" or "serve them" but **iḥsān**, doing good — far more comprehensive, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: spending to support them as needed, serving them physically when required, never talking to them in a voice too sharp or too loud, never saying anything that may break their heart, never treating their friends and well-wishers in a manner that hurts them, and doing everything possible to comfort and please them. Even if the parents have fallen short in fulfilling the due rights of their children, the children should never take that as an excuse for their own ill-treatment.

Two of the reports it gathers. Sayyidnā Muʿādh ibn Jabal said that of ten things the Prophet ﷺ asked him to be particular about, one was "do not associate anyone with Allah even if you are killed or burnt alive," and the second, "do not disobey or hurt your parents even if they ask you to leave your children and family" (Musnad Aḥmad). And in Tirmidhī: the pleasure of Allah lies in the pleasure of the father, and the displeasure of Allah in the displeasure of the father.

## Relatives, orphans, the poor

Ibn Kathir cites the ḥadīth, "Charity given to the poor is Sadaqah, while charity given to relatives is both Sadaqah and Silah (keeping the relations)." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same from Sayyidnā Salmān ibn ʿĀmir — charity to a kinsman brings a twofold reward, one for the giving, one for the rights of kinship (Musnad Aḥmad, Nasāʾī, Tirmidhī). The verse the Prophet ﷺ very often recited at the end of his sermons, still recited in the Friday khuṭbah worldwide, carries the same subject: "Allah commands you to do justice and be good to all and to fulfil the rights of the relatives" (16:90). Parents come first, then relatives in general.

Orphans are named, says Ibn Kathir, because they lost the caretakers who would spend on them, so Allah commands they be treated with kindness and compassion; the poor because they have various needs and cannot find what sustains them, so Allah commands they be helped sufficiently to end their inadequacy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the placement: their rights were treated in detail earlier in the sūrah, but recalling them here under the general head of relatives hints that helping orphaned children and helpless people should be considered as necessary as helping one's own relatives.

## The two neighbours

ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that "the neighbour who is near of kin" means the neighbour who is also a relative, and "the neighbour who is a stranger" the one who is not; Ibn Kathir notes that ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Maymūn bin Mihrān, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd bin Aslam, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān and Qatādah were reported to have said similarly, while Mujāhid was also reported to have said it means the companion during travel.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the views without choosing. Commentators generally take the close neighbour as one who lives next to your house, the distant one as living further off. Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās took the close neighbour as neighbour and relative at once — holder of two rights — and the distant as simply a neighbour. Some took the close as the Muslim and the distant as the non-Muslim. Its verdict: the words of the Qurʾān lend themselves to all these meanings, and neighbours may lawfully differ in degree of claim, by kinship or by religion — yet it is agreed that a neighbour, close or distant, related or unrelated, Muslim or non-Muslim, has the essential right to be helped and cared for to the best of one's ability.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Jibril kept reminding of the neighbor's right, until I thought that he was going to give him a share of the inheritance" — Ibn Kathir notes that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded it. Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī recorded it from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr as well, at-Tirmidhī calling that "Hasan Gharib through this route"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same teaching from al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

## The companion at your side, and the wayfarer

Sixth is the companion at your side. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it literally: a travel companion beside you in a rail compartment, an aeroplane, a bus or a car, and anyone sitting with you in a common meeting. Just as the Sharīʿah has made the rights of regular neighbours obligatory, so too the right of good company owed to someone who sits next to you for a little while in a meeting or a journey — everyone, Muslim or non-Muslim, related or unrelated, as equals. Its lowest degree: cause no pain by word or deed — nothing said that hurts his feelings, nothing done that embarrasses, annoys or troubles him: no cigarette smoke blown towards his face, no style of sitting that leaves him little room.

Seventh is the wayfarer: one who, while you are in a travel situation, comes to you or becomes your guest. Since such a stranger, Muslim or non-Muslim, has no relative or friend around, the Qurʾān — purely out of regard for his predicament as a human being — has made his right obligatory too: treating him well, as much as is possible and convenient.

## Those your right hands possess

Eighth are those whom your right hands possess. Ibn Kathir: an order to be kind to them, because they are weak, being held as captives by others. An authentic ḥadīth records that during the illness that preceded his death, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept advising his Ummah, "(Protect) the prayer, (protect) the prayer, and (those slaves) whom your hands possess" — repeating it until his tongue was still. Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The slave has the right to have food, clothing and to only be required to perform what he can bear of work" (Muslim). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that although the ayah's wording refers to the owned, by analogy and on the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ these rules cover servants and employees too: no niggardliness or delay in giving them their due salary, meals and so forth, and no burdening them beyond their ability.

## "Allah does not like the arrogant and boastful"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this closing clause of ayah 36 a unifying complement of all that precedes: anyone falling short of the rights of the eight kinds just listed must be none other than the arrogant and the proud — those with an offensively heightened sense of superiority, who love lording it over others to exact esteem from them. Ibn Kathir describes the same man: proud, arrogant, insolent, boasting to others, thinking himself better than other people, though insignificant to Allah and hated by people. Mujāhid explained the two words: the first means arrogant, the second boasting about what he has while not thanking Allah — so, says Ibn Kathir, he boasts about the bounty Allah gave him while being ungrateful for it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a narration from Sayyidnā Ibn Masʿūd (Mishkāt p. 433, via Muslim): whoever has in his heart arrogance worth the weight of a particle will not go to Paradise. Asked about people who like their clothes to be good, he ﷺ answered: "Allah is beautiful; He likes beauty. Arrogance is wanton disregard of the (other person's) right and the holding of people in contempt." That definition is the hinge: disregarding a right that is owed is precisely the arrogance the ayah condemns, and the next two ayat show it doing so in two opposite directions.

## Two ways to break the same list

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 37 as a direct continuation: it "describes the nature of the arrogant who are stingy in giving rights which it is obligatory to give, fail to understand their responsibilities, and go on to the negative extreme of persuading others to take to this bad habit through their word and deed." Ayah 38, it says, describes "another trait in the character of the arrogant" — the same person, from the other side.

**The first face: withholding.** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 37 back against the list of eight: Allah chastises the stinginess of those who refuse to spend their money on what He ordered them — kindness to parents, compassion to relatives, orphans, the poor, the relative who is also a neighbour, the companion during travel, the needy wayfarer, the slaves and servants. Such people do not give Allah's right from their wealth, and they assist in the spread of stingy behaviour. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "What disease is more serious than being stingy?" And he said, "Beware of being stingy, for it destroyed those who were before you, as it encouraged them to cut their relations and they did, and it encouraged them to commit sin and they did." (Ibn Kathir names no collection for either.)

The sharpest point is linguistic. Ibn Kathir observes that *kufr* at root means to cover something — and the miser covers the favours Allah blessed him with, in that he does not spread them; so he is described by the term *kāfir*, ungrateful, with respect to those favours, since their effect does not appear on him — in his food, his clothes, or what he gives. A ḥadīth states, "When Allah grants a servant a favor, He likes that its effect appears on him." This is why the ayah's threat of a disgraceful torment "for the disbelievers" falls where it does.

**Who was it revealed about?** A narration from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, says the verse was revealed about the Jews of Madīnah: very arrogant, miserably miserly when it came to spending money, and concealing the knowledge they had received through their Scriptures about the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and the clear signs of his appearance. Convinced of these prophecies, they still acted niggardly: they neither acted on what that knowledge required nor passed the message to others who might have acted on it. This is why *bukhl* is used here in its general sense, close-fistedness in money and in knowledge both: those miserly with what Allah gave them are ungrateful to Him and fail to acknowledge His blessings, and a humiliating punishment they cannot escape has been prepared for them. Ibn Kathir balances: some of the Salaf said the ayah describes the Jews who hid the knowledge they had about the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, and the general meaning undoubtedly includes this — though the apparent wording indicates stinginess with money, with miserly conduct in knowledge also included.

**The second face: giving to be seen.** Ibn Kathir marks the sequence: Allah first mentions the punished misers who do not spend, then those who spend to show off, to gain the reputation that they are generous, not for the Face of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: ordinarily these people hold back any spending in the way of Allah and persuade others to do the same, yet when they wish to show off before people, then they do spend. A ḥadīth states that the first three persons on whom the Fire will feed are a scholar, a fighter and a spender who showed off with their actions: the wealthy man will say, "I did not leave any area that You like to be spent on, but I spent on it in Your cause," and Allah will say, "You lie, you only did that so that it is said, 'He is generous.' And it was said" — he acquired his reward in this life, exactly what he sought.

The ayah then names the root: *they do not believe in Allah and the Last Day*. Since they do not, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, spending for the good pleasure of Allah and to earn reward in the life to come does not arise; they are the accomplices of Satan, and their end will be no different from their comrade's. Ibn Kathir explains the same words: it is Shayṭān who lured them into this evil action instead of the good deed performed as it should be, encouraging, exciting and luring them by making the evil appear good — "And whoever takes Shaytan as an intimate; then what a dreadful intimate he has!"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the balance: just as it is disgraceful to be niggardly and tardy in fulfilling due rights, so it is extremely bad to spend to show off, or on purposeless ends. A good deed aimed at applause, not done for Allah exclusively, is not acceptable in the sight of Allah — and in ḥadīth it has been declared *shirk*. Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah Almighty says: I am absolutely free of any need to have partners. Whoever does a good deed and associates in it someone else with Me, I leave him with this deed of associating partners with Me."

## "And what harm would it have done them?"

Ayah 39 turns gentle after that severity, and addresses both failures at once — the one who would not give and the one who gave for applause. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as a question asked in wonder: what conceivable harm could have affected them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent out of what Allah had given them? What is so tough, so difficult, so frightening about it? Believing and acting on them does not hurt or harm or cause any inconvenience. Why then elect to be disobedient, when the certain outcome is nothing but disaster in the Ākhirah? Ibn Kathir asks the same: what harm would it cause them to believe in Allah, go on the righteous path, replace showing off with sincerity, and await His promise in the Hereafter for those who do good and spend what He has given them on what He likes and is pleased with.

Then the seal: "And Allah is Ever All-Knower of them." Ibn Kathir: He has perfect knowledge of their intentions, whether good or evil; He knows those who deserve success, and grants them success and guidance, directing them to righteous actions that earn His pleasure; and He knows those who deserve failure and expulsion from His great mercy — utter failure in this life and the Hereafter — and we seek refuge in Allah from that evil end. Fitting, for a passage that has just described people performing for an audience: the audience cannot see the heart; the One who can decides everything.
